item.text: [{"taxonId":157960,"summary":"A wild, erect perennial herb whose native origin is not specified, devil's horsewhip is distributed throughout the tropical world and introduced as a common weed in many places. Its hairy stems and leaves carry long spikes of small green, spiny flowers, with flowering and fruiting reported from September to April.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p2"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":60146,"summary":"An annual or perennial flowering herb native to the United States, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and northern South America, marsh fleabane inhabits wetlands, coastal habitats and moist inland sites, often on salty ground. It is strongly aromatic and roughly hairy, with toothed oval leaves and clusters of bright pinkish-purple or magenta flower heads.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"In parts of the Caribbean, the leaves are consumed as medicinal tea; use is discouraged during pregnancy and advised in moderation.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p3","s1:p4"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p6"]}},{"taxonId":467323,"summary":"A climbing groundcover native to Australia, climbing saltbush spreads in vine-like, light-green branches with small, semi-succulent arrowhead leaves. Its inconspicuous green summer flowers become conspicuous tiny bright-red berries in early autumn. Early European settlers around Adelaide boiled it with other saltbushes as a substitute for greens.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Early European settlers around Adelaide boiled the plant with other saltbush species as a substitute for greens.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p2","s1:p3","s1:p4"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p4"]}},{"taxonId":58725,"summary":"An evergreen conifer with a Holarctic distribution across the cool temperate Northern Hemisphere, common juniper varies from a small tree to a ground-hugging shrub. It has needle-like leaves in threes and berry-like cones that ripen over 18 months from green to waxy blue-black. The bitter cones are not eaten raw; dried and usually crushed, they flavour meats, sauces, stuffings, beer and gin.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Bitter cones are not eaten raw; they are dried, usually crushed, and used sparingly to flavour foods, beers and spirits.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p4","s1:p5","s1:p23","s1:p24"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p23","s1:p24"]}},{"taxonId":516107,"summary":"A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, Silene marizii occurs in mainland Portugal.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p4","s1:p5"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":57162,"summary":"An annual grass native to the Mediterranean Basin, little quaking-grass forms narrow clumps of upright stems. Its young shoots are bright orange to red-brown, while its glossy dark-green needles have two chalk-white bands beneath.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p2"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":77089,"summary":"A eucalypt tree endemic to limited areas of southern South Australia, sugar gum occurs naturally in the Flinders Ranges, Eyre Peninsula and Kangaroo Island.
